name: Aaron Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight, which is early for me these days, make coffee and start on the job hunt. I've got a script that scans three job boards and emails me matches, so mornings are mostly reading those and tweaking applications with an AI assistant. Afternoons I do a free Python course and some no-code projects. Until August I was in customer support at Hartwell Home, an online furniture shop, for five years. They put a chatbot on the front line and cut the team from twenty-two to six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's mostly hype, great, but I can't say I believe it, because the chatbot at Hartwell wasn't hype. It was good enough to cost sixteen of us our jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a plateau is the polite way of saying it's a slower squeeze. I'd tell friends to learn the tools now, because a small improvement is enough to shrink a team. Online I'd say hype and layoffs can both be true at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a plateau suits me fine. It'd give me time to turn my AI skills into something paid before every desk job is gone. But my money is the problem, not AI: no savings, benefits only, and a rent bill that doesn't care about my five-year plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the Python course in about a month, then build three small projects I can show: an auto-reply checker, a ticket sorter and a job-board scraper. I'd apply to about fifteen jobs a week, mostly junior operations or support-tooling roles at companies that use AI to help support teams rather than replace them. I'd also offer to automate things for two local shops for a small fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine in daylight, uneasy at night. I know I've got skills, but skills don't pay the landlord, and there's no cushion to take a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you charge the local shops, and how do you find them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start at fifty pounds for a simple thing, like an auto-reply for bookings, and ask for a testimonial each time. I'd find them by walking the high street with a one-line pitch and by asking my cousin, who runs a barber shop. It's not much money, but it's real and it beats nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hype and layoffs can both be true. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool doesn't have to be brilliant to cost jobs. If a chatbot handles sixty percent of the easy tickets, a manager can drop three-quarters of the team and be comfortable. So the company calls it a success even when customers grumble.

say: I'd say a plateau is a **slower squeeze**, and a small improvement can shrink a team.
I'd say **hype and layoffs** can both be true.
think: A plateau gives me time to turn AI skills into **paid work**.
My problem is **money**, not AI: no savings and a rent bill that doesn't wait.
do: Finish the **Python course** in a month and build three small projects.
Apply to about fifteen **junior operations** or support-tooling jobs a week.
Offer to automate bookings for two **local shops** at fifty pounds.
feel: Fine in daylight, **uneasy at night**, because skills don't pay the landlord.
S0.quote: The tool doesn't have to be brilliant to cost jobs.
fieldNote: Understands **how partial automation** still cuts teams, even when the tool is only good enough.
Builds proof of skill through **small projects** and paid favours for local shops.
Anxious about rent despite strong digital habits and a clear plan.

steps.text: Finish the free Python course within a month
Build a ticket sorter and an auto-reply checker as portfolio pieces
Offer booking automation to two local shops for fifty pounds each
Apply to fifteen junior operations and support-tooling jobs a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's literally my last job described on a card: answering customers, checking, booking. So yes, I've already had the demo version of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, and the sensible response is to get good at working alongside the tools. I'd say the gains need to be shared, with a training budget that follows the person and not the company. I'd also say don't trust anyone who promises it's all fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my old job is gone for good, and many roles like it too, like junior admin, basic coding and support. The people who benefit will be the ones who can run the AI, not the ones it replaces. I want to be in that group, but I know there are thousands of people thinking the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise in something where a human is still needed to check the AI, like quality review for support teams, or building and maintaining the automation myself. I'd get one proper certificate, maybe in cloud basics, and keep using AI daily to learn faster. I'd do a few paid trial tasks on freelancing sites, even at low rates, to build reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised and a bit queasy. It feels like surfing a wave that could also dump me on the beach, and I've no money to cushion the fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the competition look like, with thousands thinking the same thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Crowded and fast. The edge will be having shipped something real and having a reference who says I did it on time. That's why I'd rather do five small paid jobs than one fancy course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people from the Hartwell team who didn't use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them were great with customers but never touched the dashboard beyond the basics. I feel for them, and I've been sharing my free course links in our group chat. I can't carry anyone, but I can point.

say: I'd say the sensible response is to work **alongside the tools**.
I'd say training budgets should **follow the person**, not the company.
think: My old job is **gone for good**, and similar roles too.
Winners will be the ones who **run the AI**, and thousands want that spot.
do: Specialise in **reviewing AI answers** for support teams or maintaining automations.
Earn one proper **cloud-basics** certificate while using AI daily to learn.
Take paid trial tasks on freelancing sites to collect **reviews**.
feel: Energised and queasy, like surfing a wave that could **dump me** on the beach.
S1.quote: I'd rather do five small paid jobs than one fancy course.
fieldNote: Prefers **shipped work and references** over certificates.
Shares free course links with **former colleagues**, a sign of community.
Alarmed because his exact job is the demo of this scenario.

steps.text: Offer to review chatbot answers for support teams on a trial basis

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is brutal. It's also, strangely, a bit of a rush. I'd be nervous and fired up at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments should act at the speed of the technology, which means yesterday. I'd back a basic income and a training guarantee, and I'd tell people to move fast and learn the tools now, because you can't wait for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be in the first wave of people who can't get a normal job. Everything I could apply to is exactly the work the AI does first. I'd have to make my own work, with tiny contracts and automations, and hope that my head start in the tools means something when the supply of people explodes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on building and selling small automations to local firms, and use the first six months to land at least five paying customers. I'd also line up every support scheme I qualify for, and cut costs by moving to a shared flat. I'd keep a plan B too: a hands-on trade course, because the robots arrive a few years after the thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. I'd feel adrenaline and dread together, like the night before an exam I haven't revised for. I wouldn't sleep much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the plan B trade course look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like electrical installation or heat pump fitting, where you need hands in a real house. I'd do the evening class through the college. It'd be a hedge, since the robots come about 2031, but at least it buys a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to your cousin with the barber shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin not to wait, to set up online booking and a simple loyalty system, and I'd do it for him for free. A barber needs hands for a long time, so a barber is safer than most, but the admin work still goes to software. We'd have a coffee and a plan.

I'd back a **basic income** and a training guarantee.
think: I'd be in the **first wave** of people who can't get a normal job.
I'd make my own work with tiny **contracts and automations**.
do: Land at least five paying customers for **small automations** in six months.

fieldNote: Hedges with a **hands-on trade** because of the robot delay.

Offers free help to a **cousin**, showing community instinct.

steps.text: Sell booking and reply automations to five local firms in six months
Move to a shared flat to halve the rent
Start an evening electrical installation course at the college
Register for every council and jobcentre scheme I qualify for

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is much better than two, but it's still going to be a bumpy ride. At least it's long enough for a plan with steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retool a whole workforce if we start properly, with funded retraining and real apprenticeships, not just online courses. I'd say learn the tools now while it's cheap, because later everyone will have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think five years lets me build a business that sits on top of the AI, like an agency that sets up automation for small firms. By 2031 the thinking AI will be doing most office work, so I'd need to be selling the plumbing. That's an optimistic version, but it's got moving parts I can control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a one-man automation service now, take a cloud certificate in year one, and aim for a technical operations job at a company that deploys AI. I'd save from the first pay, building up two months of rent, and use my spare time to learn how the robots in warehouses and care homes are set up. I'd also check in with Hartwell colleagues so we share leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and focused. It's like having a map with a few blank spots, which is much better than no map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest difference compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm improvising. With five years I can finish a certificate, run a small business for a couple of years, and get paid references before the crunch. Time turns a gamble into a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the blank spots on your map?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether small firms will actually pay for automation or just buy a cheap off-the-shelf tool. And whether I can get past the first no-income months without getting evicted. I'd keep a list of landlords who are decent about delays, in case.

I'd say learn the tools now while it's **cheap**.

By 2031 I need to be selling the **plumbing**.

Share job **leads** with former Hartwell colleagues.

S3.quote: Time turns a gamble into a plan.
fieldNote: Sees himself selling **the plumbing**, not competing with the AI.

Quotes are short and punchy, matching his voice.

steps.text: Start a one-man automation service for small firms this winter
Finish a cloud certificate in year one
Save two months of rent from the first pay
Share job leads with former Hartwell colleagues in our group chat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different game. I'll be forty-four, which still sounds young for a career change, and plenty of time to build things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, if we plan for it: training, income support, local investment in new work. I'd also tell young people that being adaptable matters more than any single degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a gift, with a worry attached. I could build real skill and maybe run a small company, but the gains from AI might still go to a few big firms. I'd rather be part of the group that builds the tools than the group that gets handed a pamphlet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper part-time degree or apprenticeship in software or operations, while running a small automation side business. I'd save two or three months of rent and keep a diversified plan, like some hands-on skill too. I'd also use AI as a tutor every day, so the learning compounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm and curious, though it's not carefree. Money is still zero today, and that makes ten years feel like a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in the first year differently, knowing you have ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop chasing every job posting and pick a direction, like operations for AI-using teams. I'd say yes to a longer course, because I'd actually have time to use it. And I'd pace myself, because a ten-year marathon needs sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If benefits get cut and I can't pay rent in the middle of a course. Or if the economy goes through a rough patch and no one hires juniors. I'd want an emergency stash, even a small one, and a friend or two I could crash with.

I'd say being **adaptable** matters more than any single degree.

Moves from sprint to pace in his planning.

steps.text: Start a part-time degree or apprenticeship in operations

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I'm adaptable, but two years is too short to turn skills into a stable income with no cushion. What would help is a basic income or a training guarantee, early warning from employers, and clear routes into jobs that supervise AI instead of just competing with it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that being good with the tools doesn't make a person safe. I use AI every day and I'm still on benefits. People shouldn't assume anyone techy has it figured out.

headlineQuote: Good with the tools doesn't make a person safe. I use AI every day and I'm still on benefits.
portrait: Aaron is **34**, lives alone in Norbridge, and has been on **benefits only** since Hartwell Home cut its support team in August.
He worked **five years** in customer support, and uses AI every day for job hunting and learning Python.
He's pragmatic and centre in outlook, wants **shared gains**, and builds small projects to prove his skills.
He feels the chatbot that replaced his team is exactly the **demo** of the scenarios, so he's alarmed when change is quick.
With more time he plans an **automation business** and a part-time degree.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since two years is too short to turn skills into stable income.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or training guarantee, plus early warning from employers.
Clear routes into jobs that **supervise AI** instead of competing with it.
